content: Pathology is the scientific study and diagnosis of diseases by examining organs, tissues, cells, and bodily fluids. It encompasses both the medical specialty that uses these materials to derive clinically relevant information and the broader scientific investigation of disease processes. The history of pathology can be traced back to the application of the scientific method to medicine during the Italian Renaissance in Western Europe. Early pathologists were often practicing physicians or surgeons. Over time, pathology has become increasingly specialized, and most modern pathologists focus exclusively on their field without practicing in other areas of medicine. The origins of pathology as a discipline involved the systematic dissection and examination of diseased bodies, organs, and tissues to understand the causes of death. True autopsies were rare before the Renaissance. Antonio Benivieni, an Italian physician (1443–1502), was one of the first to use anatomical dissection repeatedly to determine causes of death. Giovanni Morgagni (1682–1771), another prominent figure, published De Sedibus et Causis Morborum per Anatomen Indagatis in 1761, which detailed findings from over 600 autopsies, correlating anatomical abnormalities with clinical symptoms. By the late 1800s, a substantial body of literature had been developed on the gross anatomical findings of known diseases. Carl Rokitansky (1804–1878), a Viennese pathologist, performed or supervised tens of thousands of autopsies, epitomizing the extent of gross pathology research during this period. Microscopic pathology emerged as a distinct field largely due to Rudolf Virchow (1821–1902), often regarded as the father of microscopic pathology. Although the compound microscope had been invented about 150 years earlier, Virchow emphasized the importance of studying disease manifestations at the cellular level. His student, Julius Cohnheim (1839–1884), combined histological techniques with experimental methods to study inflammation, making him one of the earliest experimental pathologists. Cohnheim also pioneered the frozen section technique, which remains widely used in modern pathology for intraoperative diagnoses. Modern experimental pathology has expanded with advancements in techniques such as electron microscopy, immunohistochemistry, and molecular biology. These tools have blurred the boundaries of investigative pathology, as nearly all research linking disease manifestations to cellular, tissue, or organ processes can be considered experimental pathology. Pathology as a science seeks to understand the mechanisms of cellular and tissue injury, as well as the body's responses and repair mechanisms. Disease processes can be triggered or worsened by various external and internal factors, including trauma, infection, toxins, ischemia, autoimmunity, genetic mutations, or developmental errors. A recurring theme in pathology is how the body's protective responses to injury can sometimes contribute to disease processes. Understanding general principles such as cellular adaptation, cell death, inflammation, tissue repair, and neoplasia provides a framework for analyzing and understanding specific human diseases. Cells and tissues adapt to injury and stress through specific mechanisms that vary depending on the cell type and nature of the injury. Short-term responses include activating genetic programs to protect vital proteins and organelles from heat shock or hypoxia and repairing DNA damage caused by radiation or chemicals. Long-term adaptations include hyperplasia, where cell division increases tissue capacity to compensate for injury, and hypertrophy, where cells enlarge in response to stress, such as cardiac muscle hypertrophy due to increased resistance to blood flow. Metaplasia occurs when repeated damage to an organ's cellular lining triggers its replacement with a different cell type. Cell death can occur through necrosis or apoptosis. Necrosis is the irreversible destruction of cells due to severe injury, often caused by external factors like toxins or oxygen deprivation. It involves the leakage of cellular components, which can contribute to inflammation and further damage. In contrast, apoptosis is a regulated, orderly process of cell degeneration that occurs in both injury and normal physiological settings. Inflammation is a critical and complex response to tissue injury, particularly in fighting infection. Acute inflammation is a non-specific response triggered by injured tissue cells, innate immune cells, and adaptive immune mechanisms. It involves localized vascular changes, recruitment of neutrophils, and the initiation of adaptive immune responses. Chronic inflammation occurs when the acute response fails to eliminate the inciting factor. While chronic inflammation can help contain ongoing infectious threats, it can also lead to progressive tissue damage and, in some cases, predispose to cancer development. Tissue repair, as seen in wound healing, is initiated by inflammation and may begin even before the resolution of the initial insult. This process involves the formation of granulation tissue, proliferation of connective tissue cells, and angiogenesis driven by hormonal growth signals. While healing is a critical adaptive response, aberrant healing can result in progressive fibrosis, contractures, or other changes that compromise function. Neoplasia, or new growth, refers to the proliferation of cells independent of physiological processes. Examples include benign tumors and cancers. Neoplasia arises from genetic changes that cause inappropriate activation of genetic programs. Dysplasia, an early sign of neoplasia, is characterized by the persistence of immature, poorly differentiated cell forms. Interestingly, there are similarities in the gene pathways activated in cancer cells and those involved in wound healing and inflammation. Pathology as a medical specialty involves diagnosing and characterizing diseases in living patients by examining biopsies and other specimens. For instance, most cancer diagnoses are made or confirmed by pathologists. Pathologists may also perform autopsies to investigate causes of death. The medical practice of pathology evolved from investigative pathology, and many academic leaders in the field are accomplished in both basic science research and diagnostic practice. However, most modern pathologists focus on full-time diagnostic practice rather than original research. Pathologists typically serve as consultants to other physicians, often referred to as clinicians within the pathology community. In the United States and many other countries, pathologists undergo the same medical training and licensure process as other physicians. Pathology is a diverse field with various subspecialties, which differ between nations. Anatomical pathologists diagnose diseases by examining tissues and cells, often using gross and microscopic visual examination, special stains, and immunohistochemistry. Molecular biology techniques are increasingly employed to gain additional clinical information. Anatomical pathologists are the definitive diagnosticians for most cancers and many other diseases. Subfields include surgical pathology, cytopathology, molecular pathology, and forensic pathology. Clinical pathology, also known as laboratory medicine, focuses on diagnosing diseases through the analysis of body fluids. Clinical pathologists oversee laboratory operations, ensure test validity, interpret complex studies, and consult with clinicians to guide appropriate diagnostic testing. In the United Kingdom, pathologists are medical doctors registered with the General Medical Council. They complete undergraduate medical education and specialist training overseen by the Royal College of Pathologists. Training includes surgical pathology, cytopathology, and post-mortem pathology, with examinations to assess competence. Additional specialist qualifications are available in areas like pediatric pathology, neuropathology, dermatopathology, and cytopathology. Veterinary pathologists specialize in diagnosing and characterizing diseases in animals through the examination of tissues and body fluids. They may focus on diagnostic pathology or research into the biological processes underlying disease. Diagnostic veterinary pathologists are further categorized as anatomical or clinical pathologists. Anatomical pathologists perform necropsies (animal autopsies) and histopathological studies, while clinical pathologists analyze specimens like blood and biopsies from living animals. Plant pathologists investigate the causes of diseases in plants.
